new_statements.quote: TONO. Hay tres tonos: alto V́, ascendente V̌, bajo V (no se marca). /´/ 1. éphé 'guaje' 2. déhé 'agua' 3. ohkí 'hoyo'. /ˇ/ 2. kǒti 'cierra' 3. cǐ 'pulque'. no se marca 1. aní 'agacharse' 2. gwadé 'gallina' 3. kǒti 'cierra'.
new_statements.translation: TONE. There are three tones: high (V́), rising (V̌), low (V, unmarked). [examples of each in initial, medial and final position: éphé 'gourd', déhé 'water', ohkí 'hole'; kǒti 'close!', cǐ 'pulque'; aní 'bend down', gwadé 'hen', kǒti 'close!']
new_statements.citation: Lastra, Yolanda. 1989. Otomí de San Andrés Cuexcontitlán, Estado de México (Archivo de Lenguas Indígenas de México 13). México: El Colegio de México.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: (Lastra 1989, ALIM 13), printed p. 25 = PDF p. 24, rendered and read as an image: heading 'TONO', 'Hay tres tonos: alto V́ / ascendente V̌ / bajo V (no se marca)', then /´/ 1. éphé guaje 2. déhé agua 3. ohkí hoyo; /ˇ/ 2. kǒti cierra 3. cǐ pulque; 'no se marca' 1. aní agacharse 2. gwadé gallina 3. kǒti cierra. The reader's quote is this table linearised; every word and diacritic matches. I read the whole Fonología section (Fonemas pp. 21-24, Tono 25, Alófonos 26, Contrastes 27-28, Morfofonemática 29) and the Índice: there is no mention of acento/stress anywhere in the volume (text-layer a full-text search for stress/accent acento|acentua|stress|intensidad returns only the TONO lines).…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The variety is described as having three lexical tones (high, rising, low) that may occur on initial, medial and final syllables; the phonological sketch contains no statement about word stress/accent at all, so stress placement is undescribed in the accessible first-hand sources.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said (Mijangos 2020:120, second-hand, remarks that inflectional proclitics 'a veces pueden tener acento secundario' without locating primary stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms elicited from two speakers of San Andrés Cuexcontitlán (municipio de Toluca); tone examples given for word-initial, -internal and -final syllables. The San Felipe Santiago source (Hernández-Green 2022) likewise marks only tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog esta1236 [ots] has one dialect, San Felipe Santiago Otomí (sanf1263, municipio Jiquipilco); its sibling is Temoaya Otomi temo1245 [ott]. The quoted first-hand source (Lastra 1989) describes San Andrés Cuexcontitlán (municipio de Toluca), which Palancar/De la Cruz-Sánchez treat as a separate 'Western Otomi' variety alongside Temoaya and San Felipe; English Wikipedia lists the Toluca towns under Temoaya Otomi [ott], while our earlier survey and Turnbull 2017 group it with the western/Estado de México varieties — assignment to ots vs ott is not settled. Hernández-Green 2022 is unambiguously San Felipe Santiago (= esta1236) but has no prosodic statement beyond tone marking. Andrews 1949 'Temoayan Otomi' (list of works to obtain #1) is SIL work later published as 'Southwestern Otomí' of San Felipe Santiago; Glottolog may file it under temo1245.

sources.note: No stress-placement statement. p.119-120: 'el otomí de Toluca cuenta con tres tonos: bajo, alto y ascendente (Lastra, 1992: 17)'; fn. 2 summarises the tonal (Sinclair & Pike 1948) vs accentual (Leon & Swadesh 1949) hypotheses for Otomi generally; notes inflectional proclitics 'tienen tono y a veces pueden tener acento secundario'. Data second-hand from Lastra 1989/1992/2001.

sources.note: Survey of Otomi scholarship; nothing on stress for SW Estado de México varieties. p.471: 'Sobre el suroeste del Estado de México, hay muy pocos trabajos: el capítulo de Soustelle (1937) sobre el dialecto de San José del Sitio, Ixtlahuaca, una fonología muy detallada y completa de Andrews (1949) sobre el otomí de Temoaya.. y dos trabajos de Lastra uno de 1989 y otro de 1992'.
